description: Numbers, shape, proof, chance, and the structures that turn out to describe everything else.

concepts.title: Mathematics
concepts.summary: The one place where “obviously” can be proven. Simple rules, followed all the way to their consequences, keep turning out to describe things they were never designed for.

concepts.title: Numbers
concepts.summary: Counting begins as a habit and turns into a language. Whole numbers, fractions, negatives, the square root of two: each new kind of number was made to answer a question the old ones couldn't.

concepts.title: Zero
concepts.summary: Not just an empty place but a number you can add, multiply, and divide by, with one exception. Treating nothing as something is what made positional notation, algebra, and eventually computers possible.

concepts.title: Primes
concepts.summary: Numbers with no divisors but one and themselves. Every whole number is built from them uniquely, yet their pattern is elusive, and the difficulty of factoring large ones underpins much of modern encryption.

concepts.title: Pi
concepts.summary: The ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, about 3.14159, and irrational: its digits never end or repeat. It turns up far from circles, in waves, probability, and the structure of the universe.

concepts.title: Golden Ratio
concepts.summary: About 1.618: the proportion where the whole is to the larger part as the larger part is to the smaller. It appears in some plants and pentagons, and is credited with far more mystique than the evidence supports.

concepts.title: Imaginary Numbers
concepts.summary: Invent a number whose square is minus one and a whole new algebra opens. The name is unlucky: complex numbers are essential to describing waves, circuits, and quantum states.

concepts.title: Infinity
concepts.summary: Not a very large number but a different kind of thing. Some infinities are provably bigger than others, which is one of the strangest results we have, and it follows from a few lines of logic.

concepts.title: Set Theory
concepts.summary: Mathematics rebuilt from one idea: collections of things. From sets alone you can define numbers, functions, and infinities of different sizes, and it became the foundation nearly everything else is stated in.

concepts.title: Paradox
concepts.summary: A chain of reasoning that seems sound and ends somewhere absurd. Paradoxes are useful: each one marks a hidden assumption, and resolving them has repeatedly forced mathematics to grow.

concepts.title: Proof
concepts.summary: Establishing something so that no further doubt is reasonable. A proof isn't persuasion; it's a chain in which every step is forced by the one before, and anyone can check the links.

concepts.title: Incompleteness
concepts.summary: Any consistent system rich enough for arithmetic contains true statements it can't prove. It ended the hope of a single complete foundation for mathematics, and did it using mathematics.

concepts.title: Probability
concepts.summary: A way to be precise about not knowing. It turns uncertainty into numbers you can combine, update, and act on, and it's the same math that describes gases, genes, and guesses.

concepts.title: Randomness
concepts.summary: Outcomes with no pattern you could use to predict them. True randomness is surprisingly hard to define, and hard to produce; most of what computers call random is a very good imitation.

concepts.title: Statistics
concepts.summary: Learning from data despite noise. It tells you how much a sample can be trusted and how easily a pattern can be an accident, which makes it as much about doubt as about knowing.

concepts.title: Chaos
concepts.summary: Simple, exact rules can still be unpredictable in practice. A tiny difference at the start grows until it swamps everything, which is why weather can't be forecast far ahead even with perfect equations.

concepts.title: Fractals
concepts.summary: Shapes that look similar at every scale: coastlines, ferns, lightning, the edges of clouds. A very short rule, repeated, can produce endless detail.

concepts.title: Symmetry
concepts.summary: A change that leaves something unchanged. Rotate a snowflake by sixty degrees and it looks the same; swap two identical particles and the physics doesn't notice. Whole laws of nature are statements about what stays fixed.

concepts.title: Group Theory
concepts.summary: The algebra of symmetry: what happens when you combine transformations. It classifies crystals and particles, and it explains why a Rubik's cube has exactly the moves it does.

concepts.title: Logic
concepts.summary: The rules for moving from what you accept to what must follow. Reduce reasoning to switches and it can be built from transistors, which is why a very old idea now runs in your pocket.

concepts.title: Algorithms
concepts.summary: A precise recipe: do this, then this, until a condition says stop. An algorithm doesn't need to understand what it's doing, which is exactly why a machine can carry it out.

concepts.title: Geometry
concepts.summary: The mathematics of shape and space, from the surveyor's field to curved spacetime. Euclid built it from five simple assumptions; changing one of them opened whole new worlds.

concepts.title: Topology
concepts.summary: Geometry that ignores size and shape and keeps only what survives stretching: holes, connections, edges. To a topologist a coffee cup and a doughnut are the same object.

concepts.title: Calculus
concepts.summary: The mathematics of change and accumulation. It turns motion into slopes and slopes back into distance, and it gave physics its language for everything that moves, flows, or grows.
